issues.legal_issue: The reliable and corroborated portions of testimony from a witness declared hostile may be relied on to support a conviction.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were declared hostile, but each maintained that the accused assaulted the deceased; parts of their testimony identifying the assault remained unshaken in cross-examination.
Another eyewitness described the assault, and the eyewitness accounts were consistent on the material point that the accused struck the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The courts below were entitled to rely on the unshaken portions of the hostile witnesses’ evidence, which were corroborated by other reliable evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 154 of the Evidence Act, declaring a witness hostile does not efface the witness’s testimony. The reliable portions may be accepted on careful scrutiny and may support a conviction when corroborated by other reliable evidence; portions of examination-in-chief left unshaken in cross-examination may be relied on. The Court relied on Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, (1976) 1 SCC 389; Rabindra Kumar Dey v. State of Orissa, (1976) 4 SCC 233; Syad Akbar v. State of Karnataka, (1980) 1 SCC 30; Khujji v. State of M.P., (1991) 3 SCC 627; and Vinod Kumar v. State of Punjab, (2015) 3 SCC 220.

predicates.criminal_conviction_case: The proceeding concerns whether evidence supports a criminal conviction.
predicates.hostile_testimony_unshaken: A witness declared hostile maintained material testimony identifying the accused’s conduct despite cross-examination.
predicates.hostile_testimony_corroborated: Other reliable evidence supported the material part of the hostile witness’s testimony.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction case includes hostile testimony that remains unshaken and is corroborated, that testimony may support the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Eyewitness, medical, and surrounding evidence can establish beyond reasonable doubt that an accused caused a death and can disprove an asserted accidental cause.
material_facts: Eyewitnesses testified that the deceased was stopped and assaulted, including by the accused, and that the deceased cried for help.
The doctor identified a head injury as the cause of death and stated that only some injuries could have been caused by an accident.
The physical circumstances at the scene, including the condition and position of the body and motorcycle, did not support the accident account.
issues.conclusion: The accident theory was unreliable, and the evidence proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused caused the deceased’s homicidal death.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Court assessed the eyewitness evidence together with the medical evidence and the physical circumstances, and found that the evidence as a whole established an assault causing death and contradicted the proposed accident explanation.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_case and eyewitnesses_identified_assault and medical_evidence_linked_injury_to_death and surrounding_evidence_contradicted_accident

predicates.criminal_conviction_case: The proceeding concerns whether evidence supports a criminal conviction.
predicates.eyewitnesses_identified_assault: Eyewitnesses identified the accused as participating in an assault on the deceased.
predicates.medical_evidence_linked_injury_to_death: Medical evidence identified an injury as the cause of the deceased’s death.
predicates.surrounding_evidence_contradicted_accide: The physical circumstances and other evidence were inconsistent with the claim that the death resulted from an accident.

issues.definition: When eyewitnesses identify the assault, medical evidence links an injury to death, and surrounding evidence contradicts an accident account, guilt may be found proved beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings supporting a criminal conviction are not ordinarily disturbed in an appeal unless exceptional circumstances, such as perversity or material error, are shown.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a conviction affirmed by the High Court after the trial court had convicted the accused.
The Supreme Court found that the courts below had relied on sufficient evidence and that their findings were neither perverse nor affected by an illegality making them unreliable.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no exceptional basis to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court’s powers under Article 136 of the Constitution are wide, but it ordinarily does not reappreciate evidence or interfere with concurrent findings of fact in criminal appeals except in exceptional circumstances, including perversity, improper appreciation, material legal or procedural error, or findings unsupported by the evidence. The Court relied on Ganga Kumar Srivastava v. State of Bihar, (2005) 6 SCC 211, and Alamelu v. State, (2011) 2 SCC 385.

rule.if: article_136_criminal_appeal and concurrent_findings_support_conviction and not exceptional_error_in_findings

predicates.article_136_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal invoking the Supreme Court’s discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_findings_support_conviction: The lower courts made concurrent factual findings that are supported by the evidence.
predicates.exceptional_error_in_findings: The findings are perverse, materially erroneous, or otherwise unsupportable on the evidence.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal under the Supreme Court’s discretionary jurisdiction, supported concurrent findings are left undisturbed when no exceptional error in those findings is shown.
